subtitle: Person-centered practices in Minnesota begin with the person’s goals. Learn to support informed choices and connect plans with the life the person wants.
scope: For DHS staff learning about Minnesota person-centered practices. Original practice examples support understanding and reflection; they are not an eligibility decision, clinical assessment, authorized support plan or certification as a planning facilitator. Formal program, planning, privacy and reporting responsibilities remain with the appropriate roles and applicable requirements. Learning is voluntary. Private or practice reflection is welcome; no live service record or personal disclosure is required. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: Person-centered practice begins with a person’s life, not only the services available. What relationships, interests, routines and possibilities matter to this person? What support could help them pursue those things, and how will we learn whether the support is useful? Minnesota’s guidance connects these questions with discovery, planning, action and review. In this course, an original person wants to make ceramics with a friend. You will examine the meaning of that goal, compare ways to support choice and follow an honest account of what happens. Staff in many roles can use this understanding while preserving the particular responsibilities of authorized planners and service programs. Learn at your own pace and keep personal reflections private if you prefer.

lessons.title: Begin with the life the person wants
lessons.summary: Understand the meaning of a goal before replacing it with a service, appointment or attendance target.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a person’s life goal from the service activity proposed to support it.
objectives: Distinguish a person’s life goal from the service activity proposed to support it.
Explain why strengths and relationships matter to the planning question.
Choose a discovery question that preserves the person’s meaning without promising an outcome.
takeaways: The person’s interests, relationships and desired life give the support question its purpose.
An offered service is one possible means, not an automatic definition of the goal.
Discovery needs curiosity about the individual rather than a prediction from a label.
lessons.statement: A service can be useful without being the whole purpose of a person’s life.

intro.heading: Ask what the activity means
intro.body:
Minnesota’s person-centered guidance begins with a person’s desired life and the relationships, interests, strengths and supports that matter within it. The practical difference is a starting question. Instead of asking only which existing service fits, ask what the person hopes to do or experience. A service list may become relevant, but it should not replace discovery of the goal. This does not mean staff promise every requested service or outcome. It means the person’s meaning stays visible while the appropriate roles examine possible support.

In an example, Rae wants to make ceramic bowls with Leena, a friend from an earlier community class. Rae enjoys choosing colors and showing unfinished work to someone who understands the process. A staff note shortens this to “attend an activity once a week.” That description records a schedule but loses the relationship and creative choice. A quiet pottery demonstration attended alone might meet the attendance measure while missing what Rae wanted. No one needs to assume that demonstrations are bad; the issue is whether this particular option serves this particular goal.

Drew, a practice support planner, asks Rae what a satisfying visit would involve. Rae describes working at the same table as Leena, choosing the design and having time to talk while the clay dries. Rae also explains that previous experience with color mixing is a strength, not something the team must teach again before Rae can participate. These details help the planner compare possibilities. They do not establish a service entitlement, prove that a specific studio is accessible or promise that the friendship will deepen.

Person-centered practice sees the person as more than a diagnosis, support category or current program placement. A relevant support need can be acknowledged without becoming a prediction about every interest or ability. A person may value work, family, solitude, faith, friendships or activities in a different combination from the staff member. Understanding those meanings is useful even before a formal plan changes.

For your own learning, consider a practice or ordinary personal goal. What would be lost if it were reduced to a calendar entry? Reflect privately on the difference between being present and experiencing what mattered. You do not need to disclose a service history or submit a live plan to understand the distinction.

inThisLesson: A desired life and a proposed service.
Relationships and individual strengths.
A discovery question with useful detail.
Learning without a live record or disclosure.
lessons.keyStatement: Keep the person’s meaning visible when an activity is translated into a plan.

flashcards.back: What the person wants to pursue or experience, understood in its individual context.
A possible support toward the goal, subject to its actual program and authorization requirements.
Learning about the person’s interests, strengths, preferences and support needs rather than filling gaps with assumptions.
Being at a place does not by itself show that the person could take part in the experience they wanted.

items.title: Ask beyond the activity name
items.body: “Pottery” could mean making a useful object, sharing time, developing a skill or meeting new people. Rae supplies the relevant meaning here: creative work with Leena and real design choice. A planner can use that answer to compare options more accurately without deciding that every pottery participant wants the same things.

items.title: Notice strengths that already exist
items.body: Rae’s color-mixing experience can shape the opportunity and support. Treating every person as a beginner because they receive services could replace useful strengths with unnecessary instruction. The planner still checks the actual task and any support needed; recognizing a strength does not mean assuming every related task is effortless.

items.title: Preserve a question when information is missing
items.body: If the team has not asked what matters to Rae, the note should not imply that attendance is the complete goal. Ask in a suitable way and keep the unanswered part open. A positive-sounding description cannot establish a preference that the person has not expressed.

tabs.label: An attendance target
tabs.body: “Attend once a week” can help describe frequency after the goal is understood. Used alone, it could direct staff toward any scheduled activity and hide whether Rae had a creative role or time with Leena. The measure is not false; it is incomplete for this purpose. Add the experience it is meant to support.

tabs.label: A staff-selected benefit
tabs.body: “Improve social skills” changes the goal into a staff judgment about what Rae needs to become. Nothing in the example establishes that judgment. Rae wants shared creative time, not a personal deficit label. Discuss relevant support and learning if Rae chooses them without making the desired relationship depend on a newly invented problem.

tabs.label: A person-described experience
tabs.body: “Choose designs and make bowls alongside Leena” gives the team something specific to explore. A studio might support it, or another setting might fit better. The description retains Rae’s strengths and relationship while leaving availability, support and actual service decisions to be examined. It is clearer without promising success.

check.question: Which discovery question best preserves Rae’s goal?
check.correct: What would a satisfying ceramics visit with Leena involve, and what support would help you take part?
wrong: Which of our scheduled activities should replace the pottery idea?
How many social skills must you improve before you can attend?
Can we record weekly attendance as proof that the whole goal is met?
check.feedbackCorrect: The question asks about the experience and support without defining the goal for Rae or claiming an outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A service menu may matter later, but starting with replacement erases the proposed meaning. An invented skills requirement makes participation depend on an unsupported deficit. Attendance alone cannot prove that Rae had design choice or shared time. Ask about the actual desired experience.

items.text: Rae wants to choose bowl designs while working with Leena.
Rae has experience mixing colors.
A local studio may offer a suitable shared table.
An available transport arrangement could help reach the studio.
Any weekly activity will satisfy Rae’s goal.
Receiving support proves that Rae needs beginner instruction.

lessons.next: Examine how preferences and practical support needs can be considered together.

scenario.context: Practice discovery: the note says only weekly attendance. Rae explains that making something with Leena matters more than watching a demonstration alone.
options: Keep that meaning in the exploration and examine options and support with Rae.
Keep the attendance target alone because it is easier to count.
Promise that the preferred studio will be funded and available.
responses: This uses Rae’s explanation to improve the question while retaining the real decisions still needed.
Counting can be useful, but this count would miss the experience Rae described.
The goal matters; it does not establish funding, availability or authorization.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice example or private reflection to explain the difference between an activity and what it means to a person.

move.control: You can ask about the individual meaning before assuming a program label supplies it.
move.failure: A schedule is mistaken for the whole goal, and a desired relationship or creative choice disappears from the account.
move.next: If useful, write one discovery question for Rae’s practice goal. This is learning practice, not a completed formal assessment.

lessons.title: Consider what matters and what support is needed
lessons.summary: Bring preferences, practical needs and identified concerns into the same conversation without making the person’s goal disappear.
lessons.objective: Explain the difference between what is important to a person and a relevant support need.
objectives: Explain the difference between what is important to a person and a relevant support need.
Distinguish an identified concern from an unverified prediction about an activity.
Compare support options that retain the person’s goal and appropriate responsibilities.
takeaways: Preferences and necessary support should be considered together, not treated as competing labels.
Identify the particular concern and what is known before choosing a response.
Person-centered discussion does not authorize ignoring actual safety, service or reporting responsibilities.
lessons.statement: Understanding support needs can help preserve a goal rather than automatically replace it.

intro.heading: Keep the goal in the support conversation
intro.body:
Minnesota’s guidance distinguishes what is important to a person from what is important for the person. The first concerns the experiences, relationships and routines that make life satisfying to them. The second includes relevant needs for health, safety and well-being. These are not two teams in a contest, with personal choice on one side and professional care on the other. The planning question is how support can address a specific need while taking the desired life seriously. Neither a preference nor a general concern supplies every answer.

In the example, Rae prefers the Saturday studio session because Leena can attend then. The walk from the nearest transit stop includes a crossing Rae has not used before. One staff member calls the activity unsafe and proposes replacing it with a different group at Rae’s residence. Another says choice means the team should discuss no concerns. Both responses skip the specific issue: unfamiliar travel for a particular visit. The team has not established a clinical restriction, travel ability finding or legal limit. It needs information and the appropriate support-planning conversation.

Drew asks Rae what is already familiar and what would help with the journey. Rae would like information about the crossing and possible travel support before deciding. With the appropriate roles, the team can examine the route, available arrangements, timing and Rae’s questions. A possible supported visit could help Rae learn about the experience if actually appropriate and arranged. This is not an instruction for an unqualified staff member to assess travel safety or authorize unsupervised activity.

The informed-choice guidance for support planners connects goals, relevant risk, options and review. A concern should be described clearly enough to consider support, not used as a vague reason to abandon the goal. At the same time, respecting choice does not erase applicable duties, including role-specific reporting or emergency responsibilities. This course does not decide an actual risk, restriction or report. Use the responsible program and professional processes in real situations.

Privately consider how you respond when a goal and a concern appear together. Do you immediately replace the goal, dismiss the concern or ask what would help? The value of this reflection is a more complete understanding, even when the actual situation still needs another professional or an authorized decision.

A specific concern and an unverified prediction.
Options that preserve the desired experience.
Actual roles and duties in real situations.
lessons.keyStatement: Describe the concern precisely enough to explore support without erasing the person’s purpose.

flashcards.back: The relationships, experiences, choices and routines that matter to this person.
Relevant health, safety and well-being needs, considered with the person rather than used as an automatic replacement goal.
A specific issue with an evidence basis that needs an appropriate response or further inquiry.
A possible way to help with the desired experience, subject to suitability, actual responsibilities and available arrangements.

items.title: Ask what the word unsafe describes
items.body: A broad label does not explain the particular crossing, Rae’s experience or possible support. The useful inquiry identifies the known circumstance and what remains to be checked. An actual urgent danger would retain its proper response; this practice unknown does not authorize inventing one.

items.title: Choice needs usable information
items.body: Dismissing every concern as disrespectful could leave Rae without information requested for the decision. Explaining the route and suitable support possibilities can increase the substance of the choice. Do not turn that explanation into pressure to select the staff member’s preferred option.

items.title: A different activity is not always an equivalent answer
items.body: A residence-based group may be a real option, but Rae wanted creative time with Leena at the Saturday session. Compare what each alternative would and would not provide. A practical difference can be discussed without declaring one setting universally good or bad.

tabs.label: Replace the goal immediately
tabs.body: The residence activity may be simpler to arrange, but moving directly to it treats an unexamined crossing as a final answer about Rae’s desired visit. The team loses the chance to identify suitable travel support or another option that retains the relationship. Examine the specific need before presenting convenience as necessity.

tabs.label: Avoid all concern discussion
tabs.body: Saying “it is your choice” while withholding relevant information is not the same as supporting informed choice. Rae has asked to understand the journey. A respectful response includes that information and appropriate support possibilities, with real duties intact. The person should not have to choose between control and a useful explanation.

tabs.label: Explore the support and the experience
tabs.body: An appropriate planner can consider the crossing, travel arrangements, timing and Rae’s questions together. This keeps the ceramics goal visible while addressing the actual uncertainty. It does not guarantee a particular arrangement, certify travel ability or permit staff to ignore a required process.

check.question: What is the best starting response to the practice travel concern?
check.correct: Identify what is known about the journey and examine appropriate support options with Rae while retaining the stated goal.
wrong: Cancel the ceramics goal because an unfamiliar crossing proves the activity is unsuitable.
Avoid explaining the route because mentioning a concern always undermines choice.
Let an unqualified colleague certify that the crossing is safe for Rae.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response addresses the specific uncertainty and goal together while preserving the roles needed for actual decisions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An unfamiliar route is not a complete suitability finding. Withholding an explanation Rae wants weakens the choice rather than protects it. A colleague cannot gain professional assessment or authorization powers through this learning exercise. Use the relevant responsible process and person’s questions.

items.text: Rae wants Saturday ceramics because Leena can attend.
Rae asks for journey information before deciding.
Check the actual available travel arrangements through the appropriate role.
Discuss what support Rae would find useful for this particular journey.
An unfamiliar crossing makes every community visit unsuitable.
Respecting choice means hiding any relevant concern.

lessons.next: Consider whose meanings and voices shape the planning conversation.

scenario.context: Practice planning: a colleague proposes substituting the residence activity without discussing the crossing or Rae’s desired time with Leena.
scenario.prompt: Which response best keeps the planning question complete?
options: Accept the substitution because an easier arrangement must be person-centered.
Return to Rae’s goal, the specific journey question and suitable support possibilities through the appropriate roles.
Declare there can be no limits or responsibilities once Rae expresses a preference.
responses: Ease of arrangement alone does not show that the alternative fits the experience Rae wants.
This retains both the purpose and practical inquiry without a premature finding or promise.
A preference matters, but applicable responsibilities and actual decisions still remain.

lessons.transfer: In a private practice example, compare a person’s goal with one specific support need and one unanswered question.

move.control: You can preserve the purpose while making a concern specific enough to examine.
move.failure: A vague concern becomes a final denial, or a slogan about choice removes information the person wanted.
move.next: If useful, describe one possible support question for Rae’s journey. Do not treat the answer as a real risk assessment or authorized service decision.

lessons.title: Make room for the person’s voice and chosen support
lessons.summary: Understand different meanings of independence and support, and arrange participation around the person rather than an assumed style.
lessons.objective: Explain two supplied personal meanings of making a decision with or without chosen support.
objectives: Explain two supplied personal meanings of making a decision with or without chosen support.
Distinguish a chosen planning participant from someone given decision-making authority.
Choose a communication approach that helps the person express a preference without compelled disclosure.
takeaways: Independence can include asking a trusted person to help think through a choice.
The person’s communication and participant preferences need individual inquiry.
A chosen friend is not automatically a substitute decision-maker or permission to share every record.
lessons.statement: Listening to a chosen support person should not make the person’s own voice disappear.

intro.heading: Learn what support means to this person
intro.body:
Person-centered planning involves the person and the people they choose, with communication that supports their participation. A meeting invitation alone does not show that the person could understand the choices, express a preference or shape the discussion. Think about the pace, format, time and participants as part of the conversation. Formal planning responsibilities and any actual legal authority remain separate; this learning example does not determine guardianship or representation rights.

Drew initially asks Rae to make the studio decision alone to protect independence. Rae asks to talk with Leena first. In this example, Drew explains a learned meaning: in Drew’s earlier community experience, choosing without someone speaking for you was a sign of adult respect after decisions had often been made on a person’s behalf. Rae describes another learned meaning: thoughtful choices developed through reciprocal conversation, where friends offered ideas and each person remained free to disagree. Talking with Leena feels like exercising control, not giving it away. These are the individuals’ supplied histories, not profiles of nationalities or all people receiving support.

The wider understanding changes Drew’s response. Rae can choose a conversation with Leena while retaining the opportunity to express a personal position. Drew asks Rae what role Leena should have and how the options would be useful to receive. Rae chooses a short description before the conversation, time to think, and Leena as someone who can discuss the creative activity. Drew can listen to Leena’s account without recording it as Rae’s final choice. When Rae disagrees with a suggestion, that disagreement remains meaningful.

This adaptation responds to the meaning Rae explained, not merely a missing meeting detail. The practical format supports that meaning. It does not mean every person wants a trusted friend present or that one can infer a preference from identity. Another person might value discussing the options privately. Appropriate information sharing is limited to what the actual process permits and the person’s choices; selecting a participant is not blanket consent to distribute a whole service history.

For personal intercultural learning, notice how your own definition of a respectful choice developed. What have you learned about responsibility, privacy or mutual support? You may explore that question without telling anyone your history. Understanding a different meaning can be worthwhile in itself, even before a document or workplace practice changes.

inThisLesson: Individual meanings of independence and mutual support.
A chosen participant and the person’s own position.
Communication pace and format.
Private personal understanding.
lessons.keyStatement: Ask how a person wants support rather than treating your own style as the universal definition of independence.

flashcards.back: A person the individual wants involved in planning, with a clear role and appropriate information boundaries.
How an individual understands an action in light of learned experience, not a prediction from a group label.
Considering another person’s explained meaning and adjusting your interpretation rather than simply renaming your original assumption.
A suitable way to receive information and express a position, without replacing the person’s choice.

items.title: A discussion can support control
items.body: Rae can ask Leena for ideas and still choose differently. Drew’s earlier concern about being spoken for remains understandable, but it does not justify excluding a friend Rae wants involved. Ask about the preferred role and leave space for Rae’s own answer rather than treating consultation as dependence.

items.title: The friend’s answer is not automatically the person’s answer
items.body: Leena might enjoy a different studio or schedule. That perspective is useful information, not a replacement preference. Drew can ask Rae what fits and acknowledge disagreement without requiring the friends to reach one joint position before planning continues. Actual representative authority, if relevant in another case, needs its own review.

items.title: A suitable format serves the meaning
items.body: Rae’s short advance description and thinking time allow a considered conversation with Leena. A long meeting agenda may not serve that purpose. Check the individual preference and appropriate access needs; delivering a document does not prove that its content or format supported participation.

tabs.heading: Compare ways to interpret the request

tabs.label: Independence defined by the planner
tabs.body: Drew’s initial alone-first rule aims to avoid someone speaking for Rae. Yet it excludes the reciprocal discussion Rae values and turns Drew’s own experience into a universal participation standard. Keep the concern about substituted voice, but address it by clarifying roles and hearing Rae rather than forbidding chosen support.

tabs.label: Support mistaken for authority
tabs.body: If the team lets Leena choose the studio because Rae invited her, it makes the opposite mistake. The invitation gives a discussion role in this example, not decision authority. Rae’s wish to consider another view remains a choice. Record the individual preference accurately and preserve actual legal and information responsibilities.

tabs.label: A person-shaped conversation
tabs.body: The revised approach lets Rae choose Leena’s involvement, receive useful advance information, think and express agreement or disagreement. Drew learns that mutual discussion can be an expression of control here. The format and behavior change with that understanding without becoming a rule for every future person.

check.question: What best explains Drew’s change in the example?
check.correct: Drew learns that Rae’s chosen reciprocal discussion can support control and adjusts the conversation while retaining Rae’s own voice and actual information boundaries.
wrong: Drew discovers that all people from Rae’s background want family-style decisions.
Drew gives Leena decision authority because a trusted friend attends.
Drew adds a document but keeps the rule that Rae must decide alone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The interpretation and response change because of Rae’s explained meaning, not a group profile or assumed transfer of authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A supplied personal account cannot establish a universal background pattern. Friendship or attendance does not create substitute decision authority. Adding a document without revisiting the alone-first rule misses the explained meaning. Clarify the chosen role and hear the person’s own position.

items.text: Drew learned to associate choosing alone with being treated as an adult.
Rae describes reciprocal discussion as a way to think while retaining choice.
Rae chooses Leena for the planning conversation.
Rae requests a short description and time to consider it.
A friend’s presence proves the person cannot decide.
Leena may decide every service matter because Rae invited her.

lessons.next: Use the person’s perspective to compare options and the information needed for a real choice.

scenario.context: Practice conversation: Rae wants Leena’s ideas but disagrees with her preferred session time. Drew is unsure whether to record the friend’s position or Rae’s.
scenario.prompt: Which response fits the stated roles?
options: Record Leena’s position because trusted support overrides disagreement.
Require Rae to decide alone so support cannot influence the answer.
Clarify Rae’s own preference and Leena’s chosen discussion role, while retaining suitable communication and information boundaries.
responses: The discussion role does not make Leena’s preference Rae’s decision.
This removes the mutual conversation Rae chose instead of clarifying how it supports the person’s voice.
This recognizes the meaning of chosen support without transferring authority or silencing disagreement.

lessons.transfer: Privately compare two possible meanings of a respectful decision. You may use the example rather than share a personal history.

move.control: You can ask about the chosen role and respond to the meaning the person explains.
move.failure: A preferred support style is mistaken for incapacity, or the support person’s preference replaces the individual’s own position.
move.next: If useful, describe how Drew’s interpretation changed and one behavior that now fits Rae’s meaning. No personal cultural placement or public reflection is required.

lessons.title: Offer information for a meaningful choice
lessons.summary: Compare real possibilities with clear information about the experience, support, availability and unresolved decisions.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an option worth exploring from an available or authorized service.
objectives: Distinguish an option worth exploring from an available or authorized service.
Identify information Rae needs to compare two possibilities without pressure.
Choose an explanation that preserves the desired goal and honestly describes limits or unanswered questions.
takeaways: A current service list should not define every possibility worth exploring.
Information about benefits, limits and unknowns makes a choice more substantive.
Exploring an option is distinct from promising availability, eligibility or funding.
lessons.statement: An honest limit and an open possibility can be explained together.

image.caption: People exchange ideas at a table with notes and screens in front of them.

intro.heading: Compare what the options actually offer
intro.body:
Informed choice needs more than a yes-or-no question after a team has already selected the preferred answer. It involves information the person can use to compare possibilities in relation to what matters to them. Minnesota’s guidance encourages exploration beyond the current menu of services while retaining the respective agencies’ actual obligations. Those ideas fit together: a planner can take a possibility seriously without promising that every arrangement is available, funded or authorized.

Drew and Rae identify two practice possibilities. The Saturday community studio offers shared making time, but the team has not confirmed equipment access, cost or suitable travel arrangements. A weekday demonstration is available through a current activity arrangement, but Leena cannot attend and participants mainly watch. Calling both simply “pottery” hides the differences. Rae needs a clear description of making versus watching, opportunities for design choice and shared time, practical support, known costs and what is still uncertain.

An honest comparison could explain that the Saturday idea fits important parts of Rae’s goal but needs further inquiry by the appropriate roles. The weekday session is a known opportunity with a different experience. Rae may want to explore the first, choose the second for another reason or consider another possibility. The team should not frame an unknown as a guaranteed approval, or a current arrangement as proof that no other direction can ever be pursued. There may be real eligibility, funding, provider or service limits. Name the actual relevant limit and responsible decision process rather than use a vague statement that person-centered choice has no limits at all.

An experience can help the person learn, if suitable and actually arranged. For example, an appropriate visit might clarify the creative space and what support is needed. It would not itself authorize an ongoing service or prove that the studio fits every future need. Likewise, declining one visit does not mean Rae has rejected community participation. Ask what the response means in this situation.

In your own private learning, consider a choice where the options were described with one broad label. Which details would have made the difference clearer? You can practice a comparison using this example without entering costs, records or service decisions from a real person’s situation.

The experience behind an activity label.
Known limits and unanswered questions.
A comparison without pressure or a promise.
lessons.keyStatement: Describe what each possibility would offer and what still needs an actual decision or inquiry.

flashcards.back: Useful information about options in relation to the person’s preferences, support and circumstances.
A possibility confirmed in the relevant context, not automatically the best fit or an entitlement for every person.
Information still needed, kept visible rather than replaced with reassurance or a rejection.
An actual decision within the applicable program and role, separate from a learning comparison or expression of interest.

items.title: Explain the experience rather than only the label
items.body: The two pottery options involve different roles: making with a friend and watching on a weekday. Rae can judge the relevance more clearly when those differences are described. Do not add a judgment that one activity is inherently superior for everyone; the goal and choice are individual.

items.title: A specific limit is more informative than a vague no
items.body: If an actual funding or provider rule applies, the responsible role should explain it accurately and retain any applicable process. That is different from saying the studio can never be explored because it is absent from a current list. Distinguish the service decision from other possible ways to pursue the desired experience.

items.title: Pressure can hide in the presentation
items.body: Describing one option as responsible and the other as difficult could steer Rae before the actual facts are known. Explain the known differences and uncertainties without requiring gratitude for the available arrangement. The person can ask questions, disagree or want another possibility examined.

tabs.label: Only what is on the current list
tabs.body: The weekday demonstration is easy to name because it already exists. Presenting it as the only conceivable path replaces the shared-making goal with an administrative starting point. The current list still matters, but it should inform an honest explanation of possibilities and limits rather than erase exploration.

tabs.label: A promise before the facts
tabs.body: Saying the Saturday studio will definitely be funded and suitable may sound supportive. It leaves Rae relying on decisions and conditions that have not been established. A more respectful account identifies the fit, the unanswered access and cost questions, and the actual roles that can resolve them.

tabs.label: An open, specific comparison
tabs.body: The team describes each experience and distinguishes confirmed information from questions. Rae can see why the Saturday option deserves inquiry and why the weekday session is different. Real limits remain visible without being exaggerated, and exploration can continue without a guaranteed outcome or pressure to accept.

check.question: Which explanation supports the practice comparison best?
check.correct: Describe each experience, its known support and limits, and what still needs inquiry or an actual authorized decision.
wrong: Call both pottery so Rae need not consider the different experience.
Promise that the preferred studio will be approved because person-centered practice guarantees it.
Offer only the existing demonstration and treat its absence of shared making as irrelevant.
check.feedbackCorrect: The explanation makes the differences and uncertainty usable while preserving real decision responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The shared label hides making versus watching and the friend’s participation. Person-centered practice does not establish approval, funding or suitability. The existing option may be worthwhile, but it cannot silently redefine Rae’s goal. Describe the actual differences and the steps still needed.

items.text: The weekday demonstration involves watching rather than shared making in this example.
Leena is not available for the weekday session in this example.
What are the Saturday studio’s actual access, cost and support arrangements?
Which program or responsible role can address a proposed funded support?
Every desired studio arrangement must be funded once requested.
A possibility absent from the current list may never be explored.

lessons.next: Connect the chosen direction with clear action and the appropriate planning responsibilities.

scenario.context: Practice comparison: Rae asks to learn more about the Saturday studio. Its cost and suitable support arrangements have not been confirmed.
options: Keep the desired experience visible, explain the unknowns and arrange the appropriate inquiry without promising approval.
Guarantee ongoing support now so Rae will feel heard.
Stop the inquiry because the current list has a weekday option.
responses: This connects Rae’s preference with an honest next inquiry and the roles needed for real decisions.
A guarantee before the relevant facts and authorization can mislead the person.
An existing option does not prove that a different goal or possibility should disappear.

lessons.transfer: Use a private practice comparison to describe one meaningful difference, one known fact and one unanswered question.

move.control: You can distinguish exploring a goal from making an authorized promise.
move.failure: A broad label hides the choice, or a reassurance becomes a service guarantee that no appropriate role has made.
move.next: If useful, write two sentences explaining Rae’s options. Leave the actual service decision to its responsible process.

lessons.title: Connect a plan with clear responsibilities
lessons.summary: Translate the chosen direction into useful action while distinguishing general person-centered practice from formal planning and service authorization.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a general person-centered approach from a formal facilitated plan and actual program responsibilities.
objectives: Distinguish a general person-centered approach from a formal facilitated plan and actual program responsibilities.
Explain how an action, owner and agreed timing connect a support to the person’s purpose.
Identify a planning gap without treating a learning template as an authorized completed plan.
takeaways: Different programs and professional roles have different planning responsibilities.
An action needs enough detail to connect support with what the person wants.

intro.heading: Make the action understandable and keep the roles accurate
intro.body:
A person-centered approach can inform ordinary staff interactions across DHS. The formal Minnesota support-planning protocol has a particular scope, however. It identifies covered populations and responsible professional groups, with levels of accountability that vary. Its discovery, action and review principles are not a declaration that every staff member must become a case manager, perform an assessment or authorize a service. Know the applicable program and your actual contribution. A foundation course can help staff recognize a useful planning question without transferring those responsibilities.

Formal person-centered planning facilitation is also distinct from an ordinary respectful conversation. CBSM describes a skilled facilitator helping a person explore a life vision, identify steps and monitor implementation. Its disability-waiver service guidance includes an actual authorization process. A staff member does not become a qualified facilitator, gain funding authority or create an approved service plan by completing this course. Not every person wants or needs the same formal facilitated process. Preserve the applicable planning requirements while asking what support and method fit the person.

In the example, Rae chooses to pursue more information about shared making at the Saturday studio. An appropriate planner has confirmed a suitable exploratory visit and relevant arrangements within the practice process. The action account should say more than “support pottery.” Rae’s purpose is creative time with Leena and design choice. The responsible participants need to understand the agreed journey support, visit details, who will confirm changes and how Rae can communicate a different preference or an unmet need. A wish that Leena will help is not a confirmed commitment from Leena.

For learning, an action statement might describe who will check the studio arrangement with Rae and when that inquiry will return. A separate statement can record what has already been agreed. Use actual appropriate information-sharing procedures in real planning; do not send a whole private record to everyone mentioned in a learning draft. A brief plain-language account can make responsibilities clearer, but it is not a substitute for required assessments, documentation, consent, signatures or review in the applicable process.

The person’s role does not end when the plan is written. A correction about the desired experience, an unanswered support question or a changed preference can matter to what happens next. Your private practice can examine a practice action and its missing owner. No live plan or evidence of a service outcome is necessary to complete the learning.

accordion.heading: Turn a description into a usable next step

items.title: A goal is not an assigned action
items.body: “Creative time with Leena” tells the team what matters. It does not identify who will confirm the studio or what to do if the visit changes. The action account links those practical responsibilities to the goal without replacing it with an administrative task list. The person should be able to understand the relationship.

items.title: An offered role needs an actual agreement
items.body: A note that Leena will provide every journey can create a support gap if Leena never agreed. Ask about the role and capacity instead of assuming friendship means unlimited availability. The appropriate planner keeps actual support and backup arrangements clear, rather than relying on gratitude or a vague promise.

items.title: A useful document is not a compliance certificate
items.body: The course’s short action statement can reveal a missing responsibility. It cannot establish that all program-specific planning, authorization or documentation requirements have been met. Keep the learning insight and the formal process distinct so a neat page does not conceal an unfinished decision.

tabs.label: General staff practice
tabs.body: A staff member may listen to Rae’s explanation, avoid an unsupported assumption and relay a relevant question through the appropriate process. These contributions can be person-centered without making the staff member the responsible support planner. Clarity about the role protects both useful initiative and actual professional accountability.

tabs.label: Formal facilitated planning
tabs.body: A skilled facilitator can help explore a person’s life vision through an appropriate process. Where the disability-waiver service is considered, its authorization and qualification requirements remain. Calling an ordinary team conversation facilitated planning does not supply those conditions or mean every person needs that service.

tabs.label: Program support planning
tabs.body: The responsible professional connects discovery, the applicable plan, action and quality review within the actual program. Others may contribute, but the specific requirements and levels of accountability still matter. A short learning checklist is a way to notice a gap, not a replacement for the full applicable protocol.

check.question: What does the course’s practice action statement establish?
check.correct: It can clarify a proposed action and missing responsibility for learning, while the actual planning, authorization and documentation requirements remain separate.
wrong: It qualifies every learner to provide formal person-centered planning facilitation.
It proves that all program-specific planning requirements have been completed.
It authorizes Leena to receive the entire private record because she is mentioned.
check.feedbackCorrect: The learning statement is useful within its limited purpose and does not create professional, service or information authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The course does not provide facilitator qualification or an authorized service decision. A brief action cannot certify all applicable planning duties. Mentioning a friend does not authorize unrestricted record sharing. Retain actual roles and information procedures while using the example to understand responsibility.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice action statement to explain its purpose, proposed responsibility and what remains unconfirmed.

move.control: You can identify a useful contribution without claiming another role’s authority.
move.failure: A neat task list hides an unconfirmed commitment, or learning completion is mistaken for formal plan approval.
move.next: If useful, revise one practice action in plain language. Do not label the draft an approved plan or replace an actual professional process.

lessons.title: Return to the person’s experience and changing goals
lessons.summary: Review action and meaning together, keep mixed information honest and respond when the person’s needs or preferences change.
lessons.objective: Distinguish task completion from the experience the person hoped to have.

takeaways: A completed visit does not by itself prove that the person had the desired experience.

lessons.statement: Follow-up asks what the person experienced and what still matters, not only whether the activity occurred.

intro.heading: Review the experience without forcing a positive answer
intro.body:
Person-centered practice continues through action and review. Minnesota’s protocol connects implementation with the person’s goals, changes in preferences, support and barriers that remain. That is different from assuming that a written plan or completed appointment proves a good outcome. Appropriate planners use the actual review requirements and timing for the person’s situation. This learning course does not invent a universal deadline or replace that process with a private reflection.

In the practice follow-up, Rae attended the exploratory studio visit and made a small bowl. Rae liked choosing the colors, but the table arrangement left little time to work alongside Leena. The attendance and finished object are real parts of this practice account. They do not erase the relationship purpose. Rae says a different table arrangement might help for another visit. The account is mixed: part of the experience fit, and another important part remains unresolved. No one has established the cause of every difficulty or the suitability of a continuing service.

Drew can explore the table question with Rae and the appropriate participants, retain any actual support needs and address the plan through the responsible process. Rae may choose to continue, change the idea or pursue another direction. The person is not obliged to prove gratitude, stay with the first option or describe the visit as a success because staff made an effort. Staff effort and a valuable contribution can be recognized without asking Rae to suppress the unfinished part.

The action account also needs care. “The visit occurred” is different from “every agreed support was delivered” or “the goal was fully achieved.” If no one knows whether an arrangement was available or whether the person had time to choose, that information is missing. Silence or the absence of a complaint cannot supply the answer. Use an appropriate way to ask, and keep privacy and actual records processes intact. A public story about a person’s success would need its own appropriate permission and information review; learning does not require publishing one.

For your own understanding, return to a private practice goal from the first lesson. What result would tell you about the meaningful experience, and what would only count an activity? You can appreciate the difference without producing a live outcome. The purpose is to become more capable of noticing the person’s meaning, a useful support and an honest next question.

Mixed evidence and missing information.
Changed preferences and appropriate review.

lessons.keyStatement: Recognize the part that worked without closing the part the person says is still open.

flashcards.back: A stated action occurred; this is not proof that every desired experience or support need was met.
The individual’s description of what mattered, what fit and what they would like to change.
Different parts of an experience have different outcomes, so one positive fact cannot stand for the whole.
The appropriate process for learning about action, support, barriers and changed goals under actual requirements.

items.title: The bowl and the relationship answer different questions
items.body: The finished bowl shows a creative activity occurred in the example. Rae’s account shows that shared making was limited. Both belong in understanding the experience. A single output cannot prove that a relationship goal, access need or support arrangement was satisfied.

items.title: A changed preference is useful information
items.body: Rae might want a different table, another studio or another activity. This is not automatically failure or ingratitude. The appropriate planner explores what has changed and what support or decision is needed, while actual responsibilities and applicable review requirements continue.

items.title: No answer is not a positive answer
items.body: If Rae has not had a suitable opportunity to respond, the experience remains unknown. Do not fill that gap with a success statement because no complaint was recorded. A useful review recognizes missing information and seeks an appropriate way to hear the person without pressuring disclosure or a preferred response.

tabs.label: The activity-only account
tabs.body: “Rae attended and finished a bowl” records meaningful action but says nothing about the shared table purpose. Used as the whole result, it could lead the team to repeat an arrangement Rae wanted changed. Keep the output and add the person’s account of the experience and the open question.

tabs.label: The forced success account
tabs.body: “Rae should be happy because everyone worked hard” asks the person to validate staff effort instead of describing the result. Gratitude cannot establish that the support or relationship goal was met. Acknowledging effort is compatible with listening to what Rae found useful and what remains unresolved.

tabs.label: The mixed, person-informed account
tabs.body: “Rae liked the color choice; shared making was limited, and the table arrangement needs review” makes both parts clear. It supports the next inquiry without assigning every cause, promising a future outcome or treating the first visit as a permanent answer. Actual planning and service decisions stay with their responsible roles.

check.question: What can Drew conclude from the practice follow-up?
check.correct: The visit and color choice occurred, while Rae’s desired shared-making experience remains partly unresolved and needs appropriate review.
wrong: The finished bowl proves every goal and support need was met.
Rae must keep the arrangement because staff worked hard to organize it.
No complaint from another participant proves the experience was suitable for everyone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion stays with the stated action and individual account while keeping the open part visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A finished object does not prove every experience or support need was met. Staff effort does not make the person’s preference fixed or require gratitude. Another person’s silence cannot establish their experience, much less everyone’s. Use the limited information and continue the appropriate inquiry.

items.text: Rae attended the exploratory visit and made a bowl in this example.
Rae enjoyed choosing colors but wanted more shared making time.
The table arrangement needs an appropriate inquiry with Rae.
The responsible planner retains actual review and information requirements.
Attendance proves that every important part of the goal was achieved.
Silence from other people means that every person was satisfied.

lessons.next: Continue learning through the person’s perspective, practical support and honest follow-through.

scenario.context: Practice review: Rae describes a useful color-choice experience and an unresolved shared-table problem. A colleague wants to record the visit as fully successful.
options: Record complete success because the bowl is visible.
Record total failure and assume the table caused every possible problem.
Record the part Rae valued and the unresolved shared-making question, and continue the appropriate review without a wider guarantee.
responses: The output does not answer the relationship and participation question Rae raised.
The mixed account does not support a total-failure label or universal causal conclusion.
This preserves the person’s experience and a useful next responsibility within the information available.

lessons.transfer: Privately explain one difference between counting an activity and learning about the person’s desired experience.

move.control: You can keep the person’s account, completed action and unanswered question distinct.
move.failure: A visible output closes a question it cannot answer, or the person is pressured to report success for someone else’s reassurance.
move.next: If useful, write a brief mixed-result account for Rae’s fiction. This is reflective practice, not an actual service review or public success story.

jobAid.subtitle: A plain-language companion for understanding goals, choices, support, action and review.
remember: The person’s desired life supplies the purpose; a service or activity is one possible means.
Ask about this individual’s meanings, preferences, strengths and useful support.
General person-centered learning is distinct from actual planning, assessment, facilitation, eligibility and service authorization.
Keep actual privacy, reporting, access and program responsibilities intact.
Private or practice reflection is valid learning; no personal disclosure, live plan or public story is required.

items: What experience, relationship or direction matters to the person?

sections.heading: Support a substantive choice
items: Ask how the person wants to receive information and who they choose to involve.
Clarify a chosen participant’s role without assuming substitute decision authority or unrestricted information sharing.
Explain what each option offers, relevant support, actual limits and unanswered questions.
Consider the specific concern with the goal, using the appropriate responsible process rather than a vague prohibition or promise.

sections.heading: Connect action and follow-through
items: Keep the desired experience connected to each proposed action.
Clarify actual responsibilities, confirmed commitments and appropriate timing; do not assume an unpaid friend will do everything.
Distinguish a learning draft from the full applicable plan, authorization, documentation and review requirements.
Ask what the person experienced and what has changed, keeping mixed results and missing information honest.

sections.heading: Know the scope
items: Use the actual program guidance to identify covered populations, professional roles and applicable planning requirements.
Formal planning facilitation and service authorization have their own qualifications and processes; completing this course does not supply them.
Retain the actual role-specific reporting, emergency and other responsibilities in real situations.
Refer Native American and Tribal-specific matters to the appropriate office within ADSA; this course does not teach or decide those matters.
